The episode sits atop broader unresolved questions about whether U.S. chip technology has reached China improperly and how much latitude corporate leaders have when national security concerns intersect with presidential politics.

facts: A federal grand jury in Minnesota is hearing evidence in what prosecutors call a "pre-indictment investigation" of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.; no charges have been filed.
There are two separate probes: an immigration-fraud investigation that reportedly began under the Obama administration, and a finances investigation opened under the Biden administration.

Unsealed court records use three name variants for Omar — Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and, in a warrant return, Ilhan Nur Said Elmi Mohamed — with no explanation given for the differences.

A DOJ brief dated Oct. 7 covers alleged violations from 1980 to the present and examines whether a false name or birthdate was used to obtain U.S. citizenship; Omar has said she was born Oct. 4, 1982, a date corrected by her staff in May 2019 from a previously listed 1981 birthdate.
Federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home on Oct. 12, 2026, and seized her phone.

Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh required procedural safeguards letting Omar assert Speech or Debate Clause privilege before agents reviewed materials; DOJ agreed to this protocol but later argued a differently handled, similarly situated warrant involving another individual did not require the same steps.

Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered partial unsealing of redacted search-warrant documents, made public Monday night, while keeping the underlying affidavit sealed; the DOJ had opposed unsealing while the probe is active.

ladder.analysis:
This story sits at the intersection of an unresolved criminal investigation and a legal fight over how much the public can see while that investigation is ongoing. The grand jury's involvement signals the probe has moved into a more formal phase, though prosecutors have not disclosed what evidence has been presented or whether an indictment will follow. The naming discrepancies and birthdate questions matter because derivative citizenship through a parent's naturalization depends on the applicant being a minor at the time — a 1981 birth year versus 1982 changes whether Omar would have still been under 18, which is central to the immigration-fraud inquiry.

The unsealing dispute adds a second, procedural layer: DOJ argues Judge Boasberg applied inconsistent standards between this case and his 2023 ruling keeping search-warrant materials sealed during the Trump-related Jack Smith investigation, even though Trump had already been indicted at that point and Omar has not. The case also raises Speech or Debate Clause questions, a constitutional protection for lawmakers' legislative work, which a magistrate judge said required extra safeguards during the search — a protection not at issue in the earlier Trump ruling.

rep: Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said "where there's smoke... there may be fire," arguing that an Obama-appointed judge's scrutiny of law enforcement's probable-cause showing suggests there was sufficient basis for the search.

The DOJ argued in court filings that Judge Boasberg's decision to unseal Omar-related search warrant documents contradicts his own 2023 ruling keeping Trump-related search warrant materials sealed during an active investigation, a characterization DOJ confirmed as accurate to Fox News Digital.

ladder.steelman: Both the government's push for secrecy and the press's push for access reflect genuinely competing interests — protecting active investigations from compromise versus ensuring judicial transparency — and the core dispute is less about Omar's guilt or innocence than about whether courts are applying sealing standards consistently across politically sensitive cases.
ladder.implications: The grand jury's next moves — whether it returns an indictment or the investigation closes without charges — will determine whether this becomes a criminal case or remains an unresolved inquiry. stories.headline: Army detonates lead azide in Iowa; Vance blames Obama for lead threat

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound.
The explosives had been in storage for about 20 years.
The explosives had degraded through a process called recrystallisation.
The degradation made the explosives more prone to accidental detonation from friction or movement.
An appeals court on Monday overturned a prior ruling that had halted the detonation.

Officials estimated airborne lead dust could travel up to 100 miles depending on weather.

Officials, including President Trump, called the operation a success.
Authorities announced additional monitoring of meat, poultry and eggs amid concerns about potential effects on the food supply.
Vice President Vance, speaking to reporters in Ohio, said the Obama administration began storing the material in 2009.
Vice President Vance stated 'the can had been kicked down the road.'

The event centers on a decades-old stockpile of lead azide — a detonator compound used in ammunition — that had chemically degraded to the point the Army said it risked exploding on its own. stories.headline: US announces sweeping new tariffs on China, EU, and other trading partners
body: The Trump administration on Wednesday announced a new round of tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, India, South Korea, and Vietnam, following an eight-month investigation into alleged unfair trade practices. The highest rate, up to 40%, applies to China, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with other jurisdictions facing either 20% or 25% duties. The new taxes, which are not expected to take effect until next year, come after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs illegal in February, prompting the White House to launch a probe under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974.

The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. Mexico and Norway were also part of the investigation but were excluded because probes into their practices are ongoing. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs would 'level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy,' accusing many trading partners of adopting industrial strategies that include 'targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression' and 'other market distorting practices.' Some rates will be effectively reduced due to caps Trump has agreed to, and individual countries face different levies. About $30bn of Chinese imports are under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

Economists have warned that tariffs can fuel inflation and push up prices for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade. Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the announcement was 'not as alarming as it looks' because the taxes are 'essentially replacing' previously announced tariffs from the summer, adding that 'the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods are also not subject to these new tariffs.' US markets fell on the news: the tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 3.9% in early trading, the S&P 500 dropped 2.8%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped 1.4%. Gold prices fell more than 3% to a more-than-one-year low, influenced also by inflation data showing a 0.3% rise in a key Federal Reserve metric. Bond yields in the US and Europe dropped, with Germany's 10-year yield sliding 4.5 basis points to 3.2% and the US 10-year Treasury note yield falling 6.8 basis points to 4.834%.

The European Commission rejected the new tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for imposing them and pointing out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed. 'We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity,' said spokesperson Olof Gill. China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun denied allegations of overcapacity, calling it 'a false issue' and urging stable relations. The Swiss government rejected the investigation's allegations. Norway, which was excluded from the tariffs, welcomed the decision, with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide stating, 'Norwegian companies produce in response market demand.' The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and AI race. Despite a recent meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, no announcement was made on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

In a separate announcement, the White House also proposed a 10% tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers, and plans to raise duties on Brazilian sugar imports that exceed quotas. Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at Georgetown University Law Center, called the administration's use of Section 301 'cynical,' saying it was designed to allow the president to set tariffs globally and strip Congress of its constitutional authority. Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, noted that the timing before the G20 in mid-December 'sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027.'

stories.headline: Ukraine says its laser system downs Russian jet-powered drone in world first
body: Ukraine announced on November 25 that its Blysk laser system had intercepted a Russian jet-powered Geran drone in combat for the first time, marking a milestone for experimental air-defense technology. The claim was made by presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, who said the system, deployed by the company Carmine Sky, was protecting a critical infrastructure facility.

Beskrestnov cautioned against overoptimism, stating: "It is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser. Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities." The Blysk laser has a reported power output of four kilowatts and an effective range of up to one kilometer. Persistent cloud cover and fog over Kyiv had previously prevented the system from engaging Russian drones effectively, as lasers suffer in poor weather and cloud cover can disperse the beam.

The development comes as laser weapons are increasingly seen as a cheaper alternative to conventional air-defense missiles, with Israel's Iron Beam among the most prominent examples. Carmine Sky announced on November 19 that Ukraine's first air-defense laser had been deployed to help protect Kyiv from Russian drones, offering a potentially lower-cost method that requires electricity rather than more costly interceptor drones or missiles. However, precision tracking of agile drones with a laser remains challenging.

Beskrestnov said the technology is being developed under the "Private Air Defense" state program with support from the Brave-1 defense technology cluster. Launched by the Defense Ministry, the program authorizes companies to form air-defense groups under the Air Force's operational control. Currently, about 100 companies nationwide have joined the effort, with half forming active combat units using systems ranging from interceptor drones to automated gun turrets.

Ukrainian postal and courier company Nova Poshta, for example, has started its own private air-defense force and shot down Russian attack drones targeting their facilities, according to Vyacheslav Klymov, co-owner of the Nova group of companies. As of October 14, private air-defense units had shot down more than 60 Russian aerial targets, primarily drones, according to Ukraine's Defense Ministry. Then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said of the initiative: "We created a model where the state, military and business work as one system."

stories.headline: Poland to Establish No-Fly Zone on Ukraine Border, Urges NATO Allies to Follow
body: Poland announced on November 25, 2026, that it will create a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and called on other NATO members to do the same along the alliance's eastern flank. Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said an ordinance is being prepared and should take effect at the end of December or the beginning of January. The move comes after repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace amid Moscow's ongoing war against Ukraine. Poland already strictly limits air traffic at the border; the new zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory and provide additional support for the armed forces.

The announcement coincides with a series of military and diplomatic developments in the nearly five-year-old conflict. Ukraine's General Staff reported that its forces attacked the Russian Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region, damaging three MiG-31 jets, used to launch hypersonic missiles, and two Su-34 fighter-bombers, knocking them out of operation for some time. Russia did not immediately comment. Overnight, both sides struck energy infrastructure: Russian attacks shut down a thermal power plant and a gas production facility in Poltawa, causing power outages in five regions; Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region, killing one person and sparking large fires.

In Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate, arguing that Russia wants more than Ukraine and is escalating in the Baltic region, Poland, the Black Sea, in space, and inside Germany. 'Anyone who doesn't see that doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims,' Merz said, rebuking opposition parties—the Left Party and Alternative for Germany—that have called for ending aid. He stressed that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself.

Russian officials reiterated their demand that European diplomats travel to Moscow to explain their intentions before they can participate in any peace negotiations. Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said no Europeans have accepted the invitation, which President Vladimir Putin extended last month. Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev called the reaction 'restrained,' claiming Europe is the impediment to stopping the war and that Moscow does not see the same 'honesty' from Europeans as from the Trump administration's representatives.

Allies remain divided over Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian ships off the coast of Libya. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot defended Kyiv's actions as an exercise of its 'absolute right to self-defense,' noting Russia's ongoing aggression. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, however, called it a 'mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty' and said Italy was unaware of Kyiv's plans. Tajani said he conveyed Italy's concern to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha while reiterating Rome's support for Ukraine's sovereignty.

Separately, a German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday. Prosecutors charge her with providing sensitive information to a Russian Embassy employee—the country's former deputy military attaché, who has since been expelled—and attempting to recruit individuals from Germany's Defense Ministry and arms industry. stories.headline: Leaked data shows over 700,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war
body: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine, according to a new projection based on leaked official data from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat. The estimate, published by the exiled Russian outlet Meduza, projects a total of 720,000 military deaths, including those not yet recorded. The leak, released earlier this month by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers, contains nearly 30 million death records from early 2021 through September 2026. Independent media including the BBC and Mediazona analyzed the data and arrived at a figure of at least 490,000 registered military deaths as of the end of September.

The Rosstat dataset, which the Kremlin acknowledged was obtained through a cyberattack but denied any protected information was leaked, includes ages, places of residence, places of death, and circumstances of death. Analysts filtered the records by location, cause of death, and demographic criteria to isolate military fatalities. They identified 425,174 entries with an explicit military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat, and added 14,093 entries identified by employment records and 51,067 entries based on court rulings declaring soldiers dead after going missing for more than six months. The data was cross-checked against Mediazona's own named list of war dead, matching 95% of records, as well as official registries. Mediazona said fabricating a dataset of this scale would be 'impossible' and expressed confidence the data is genuine.

Meduza's projection of 720,000 deaths accounts for a significant lag in military death registrations, which has grown dramatically since 2024. The outlet used epidemiological methods and actuarial science tools, such as the 'chain-ladder method,' to estimate deaths that have occurred but have not yet appeared in the data. The BBC's own analysis of the leaked files found that at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war. The BBC's separate named list, compiled from open sources, stands at 290,012 deaths, but military experts estimate that figure represents only 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The data reveals stark demographic and regional impacts. In 2025, 65% of Russian men aged 18-24 who died lost their lives in the war, and 59% of those aged 25-34. The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 by 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks. Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia, such as Tyva, Buryatia, and Zabaykalsky Krai, account for a disproportionately large share of losses, with men there 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of Moscow or St. Petersburg. At least 5,017 foreigners are among the dead, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. The BBC also identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died repelling a Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024, based on satellite imagery and official photographs of a new memorial in Pyongyang.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the analysis on Wednesday, saying, 'The only department authorized to officially release data on casualties is the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation. I suggest disregarding any other data.' The Russian Defense Ministry has not officially updated its death toll since the early months of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu put it at nearly 6,000. Ukrainian losses were last estimated by President Volodymyr Zelensky at about 50,000 in July 2026, though analysts consider that an undercount; an anonymous open-source website puts the figure at 115,952, and a Center for Strategic and International Studies assessment earlier this year suggested up to 150,000 Ukrainian soldiers killed. The war, now in its fifth year, shows no sign of ending despite pressure from President Donald Trump for Kyiv to negotiate.

stories.headline: Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Accelerated to 3.8% in October, Virtually Assuring a December Rate Hike
body: The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure accelerated in October, reinforcing expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates at its December meeting and raising questions about how much more tightening may be needed in 2027. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.8% in October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly double the Fed's 2% target, according to a Commerce Department report released Wednesday. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September's figure.

Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core PCE inflation stood at 3.3%, 0.1 percentage point above forecasts. While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends. Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, matching the pace of price increases but falling 0.1 percentage point short of expectations. Personal income surged 0.7%, far exceeding the 0.4% estimate, and the personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.

A separate Commerce Department report showed the economy grew at a much stronger-than-previously-estimated 4.3% annualized rate in the third quarter, driven by upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government outlays. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of economic activity, rose 4.2% in the quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers—a key indicator of underlying demand closely watched by Fed officials—jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point. The strong growth adds to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not yet restraining economic activity.

The Labor Department also reported that initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and near the lowest level since the late 1960s, against a Wall Street forecast of 200,000.

Markets fully priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate hike at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting. However, expectations for further increases in 2027 eased slightly: traders continued to price in two more hikes but lowered the odds of a third to about one in three, down from 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. Stock market futures added to losses after the release, while Treasury yields fell sharply.

"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for about 5½ years. It had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs have continued to exert upward pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, and Japan. While policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded. "America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.

stories.headline: Nvidia stock slides as AI doubts persist despite Jensen Huang's return
body: Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 23 after resigning on Nov. 12 over reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. His return sent Nvidia shares surging.

President Donald Trump told CNBC he intervened to bring Huang back, saying, 'We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius.' Trump warned that Huang could hypothetically have taken a job in China, though he acknowledged 'never even a suggestion' that the founder was recruited by China.

The turmoil around Huang's future highlighted the U.S.-China AI race, which is about more than semiconductors. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research. 'Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack,' said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. Chinese companies are 'very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S.,' said Rachel Wu of Tidalwave Solutions, noting that a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000) plus stock options.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, who has convened an AI task force, acknowledged the outlook is 'moving rapidly and is deeply uncertain.' Markets may be rethinking the potential earnings upside and spending on AI buildout, while the adoption rate and economic effects on inflation and growth remain unclear. Warsh has pushed for the Fed to rely more on market signals than forecasts, but the Nvidia situation shows 'markets can be very short-term about the long-term signals they send,' according to CNBC's Steve Liesman.

Huang founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors later became used to mine cryptocurrencies and now train cutting-edge AI models. Trump said Huang 'has other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about.'

stories.headline: MLB sues players' union, asks court to declare lockout legal
body: Major League Baseball on Wednesday filed a lawsuit against the MLB Players Association, asking a federal court to declare that a planned lockout is legal. The league's legal action comes less than a week before the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, with a lockout expected to begin on that date barring a dramatic change in negotiations.

The lawsuit names all 30 teams as plaintiffs and lists the union along with eight players on the MLBPA's executive subcommittee as defendants: Paul Skenes, Tarik Skubal, Chris Bassitt, Jake Cronenworth, Pete Fairbanks, Cedric Mullins, Marcus Semien and Brent Suter. The league is seeking to preempt antitrust litigation that the union could file if it temporarily disbands, allowing players to sue MLB for blocking them from playing.

The filing immediately created awkward situations for several players. Skubal, who recently agreed to a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets — the richest pitching deal in baseball history — is now being sued by his new employer. Skenes, the face of the Pittsburgh Pirates franchise, is also a defendant in a federal lawsuit brought by that same organization. Suter, who just signed a one-year, $4 million deal with the New York Yankees, joins Skubal in an uncomfortable position with a new team.

The players association responded sharply, issuing a statement that called the lawsuit "completely frivolous." The union said it "will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing."

The two sides remain far apart on a new collective bargaining agreement with the deadline days away. A lockout in December appears guaranteed, and the legal battle adds a new layer of acrimony to what is shaping up to be the ugliest offseason in years.

stories.headline: Aaron Rodgers benched by Steelers, accuses coach Mike McCarthy of sleeping in meetings and saying '1, 2, 3, Packers' at halftime
body: The Pittsburgh Steelers have benched four-time NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers, making Mason Rudolph the starting quarterback for Friday's home game against the Denver Broncos, the team announced late Tuesday. Rodgers, 42, will be inactive for the game and will not serve as backup. The decision was a coaching move, according to ESPN, and Rodgers was not listed on the team's injury report. The Steelers (6-4) have lost two straight games, including a 19-16 defeat at the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.

On Wednesday, Rodgers appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and unleashed a series of accusations against Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy, who previously coached Rodgers for most of his 18-year tenure with the Green Bay Packers. Rodgers claimed that McCarthy arrived late to a quarterback meeting last Wednesday and began snoring within 10 minutes, then left the room after doing so again. Rodgers also said McCarthy missed an offensive meeting Thursday, a walkthrough Friday, and a morning meeting Saturday. Rodgers alleged that McCarthy admitted to not watching film on the Broncos in preparation for Friday's game.

Rodgers said his breaking point came at halftime of Sunday's loss to the Eagles, when McCarthy told the team, '1, 2, 3, Packers!' — a chant from his Green Bay days. NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported that multiple sources confirmed the '1, 2, 3, Packers' comment was true. Rodgers said he confronted McCarthy on Tuesday, offering an ultimatum that if changes were not made — including McCarthy relinquishing play-calling duties — he would rather not be the team's quarterback. McCarthy denied the allegations, Rodgers said. Rodgers added that his time with the Steelers is over, saying, 'That ship has sailed.'

Rodgers joined the Steelers in 2025 after two seasons with the New York Jets. He had said he was '99% sure' he would retire after leading Pittsburgh to the playoffs last season but was persuaded to return by McCarthy's hiring. The Steelers rank 22nd in both points and passing yards per game. Wide receiver Michael Pittman is injured, and DK Metcalf was ejected during Sunday's loss. Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, has won the MVP award four times (2011, 2014, 2020, 2021), second only to Peyton Manning's five. The Steelers (6-4) hold the final AFC playoff spot, trailing the division-leading Cincinnati Bengals (7-3).
Rodgers said teammate Pat Freiermuth informed him of the benching. The Steelers have seven games remaining, and it remains unclear whether Rodgers would return to the lineup if Rudolph struggles.

stories.headline: NBA Announces $11B Arena Initiative to Develop European League with FIBA
body: The NBA on Wednesday announced an approximately $11 billion initiative to construct and renovate arenas and surrounding entertainment districts in Europe, a major step toward launching a new professional basketball league on the continent alongside the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) by 2027.

The funding, backed by investment firms including Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners and J.P. Morgan, will be used to develop modern facilities that include housing, workplaces, restaurants, retail and public spaces. The NBA said the initiative aims to provide prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to sustainable capital and the league's expertise to elevate the fan experience and attract more live events.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement, 'We've seen firsthand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities. As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events.'

The league cited a study estimating the new league could drive more than $26 billion in gross value added to GDP across Europe, support nearly 15,000 full-time equivalent jobs annually, and attract nearly 70 million spectators over its first 10 years. The investors issued a joint statement expressing a commitment to honoring the passion and traditions of European basketball fans while supporting lasting economic growth.

The announcement follows a timeline confirmed in October by the NBA and FIBA targeting a 2027 launch. Previous plans for a merger with the existing EuroLeague were rejected by EuroLeague owners, who reportedly felt undervalued by the NBA and FIBA. The NBA said it will continue discussions with interested investors and arena developers as it finalizes the initiative.

stories.headline: Physicists trap single positron near absolute zero in antimatter breakthrough
body: Physicists at Northwestern University have captured a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron, and cooled it to a temperature of approximately 300 millikelvins (0.3 degrees above absolute zero) while suspending it in a wall-free trap using electric and magnetic fields. The achievement creates what the team calls a "one-positron quantum cyclotron" that allows precise manipulation of the particle's quantum energy states. The research lays the groundwork for the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between matter and antimatter.

Positrons are produced naturally during radioactive decay; the researchers used the rare isotope sodium-22 as their source. These positrons initially carry tremendous energy, which the team reduced before directing the particle into a near-perfect vacuum trap at cryogenic temperatures. Under these conditions, the positron settles into its lowest quantum energy state and can be held for months at a time. The trap uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields to keep the positron isolated from any physical container walls, preventing the annihilation that would occur if matter and antimatter touched.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Gerald Gabrielse, Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern and director of the Center for Fundamental Physics, who led the study. "The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out." Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that electrons and positrons should behave as nearly perfect mirror images—identical except for opposite charge. Gabrielse's group previously used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to measure the electron's magnetic moment with a precision of about one part in 10 trillion, one of the most accurate measurements ever performed on an elementary particle. The team now intends to perform the same measurement on the trapped positron. Any discrepancy between the two values would signal a crack in the Standard Model and could help explain why the universe contains vastly more matter than antimatter.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere—or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down." The researchers demonstrated they could deliberately change the positron's quantum energy states using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, a capability essential for the forthcoming comparison. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565), and the full study (DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj) is available in Physical Review Letters.

stories.headline: Physicists extend Einstein's theory of particle motion to explain heavy quarks in primordial plasma
body: Physicists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Santa Barbara have developed a theoretical framework that extends Albert Einstein's 1905 theory of Brownian motion to account for the behavior of particles traveling at nearly the speed of light, a regime where the century-old model breaks down. The new calculations, published in Physical Review Letters, predict that heavy quarks moving through quark-gluon plasma—the ultra-hot state of matter that filled the universe microseconds after the Big Bang—experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein's traditional model cannot fully explain.

Einstein's 1905 theory described how particles suspended in a fluid move due to a balance of drag and countless random pushes from surrounding atoms and molecules. That framework, which has been applied to many fluids including quark-gluon plasma, assumes that the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve, with moderate pushes being most common and extreme pushes becoming exceedingly rare. However, the MIT and UCSB researchers found that for particles moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. "Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," said Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing."

Du Plessis and co-author Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the strong nuclear force while moving close to the speed of light through a gas of weakly interacting quarks and gluons. They found that for small changes in momentum, the probability curve resembled the familiar bell-shaped distribution. But for larger changes, the distribution was tilted: unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed, and powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicts. "The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis said. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions."

The researchers repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found the same tilted distribution regardless of composition. They also recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely. This suggested the effect may be a universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids. "This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis said. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks."

The findings could help physicists learn more about the internal structure of quark-gluon plasma, which scientists briefly recreate in particle accelerators by colliding ions at speeds approaching light. These tiny droplets of plasma survive for only tens of septillionths of a second. By comparing the new predictions with accelerator experiments, researchers may uncover details about the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Big Bang. Du Plessis suggested that the primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas." stories.headline: FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites for orbital data center project
body: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites under the company's "Starmind" initiative, designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, the constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. The decision marks the first approval the agency has granted for a full constellation of AI satellites, with other companies including Google and Blue Origin also pursuing similar concepts.

SpaceX has described Starmind as a way to "capture solar energy in space to power" AI capabilities on Earth, transmitting data using high-speed lasers that connect to its existing Starlink network. The company plans to produce chips for the satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility. The FCC authorization gives SpaceX a long regulatory runway: the company has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite, until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and until November 2040 for the full constellation.

The authorization includes several conditions. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into "Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits" rather than burning up in Earth's atmosphere. The FCC deferred that request, saying SpaceX has not provided "sufficient information" about its disposal process plans.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement: "The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people. This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth." The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

While the announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. The FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through those remaining issues. Separately, Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space with the launch of a "Project Suncatcher" AI server satellite last month, and Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

stories.headline: Back-to-back measles deaths in US; tally now at 14
body: The United States has recorded two more measles deaths in consecutive days, bringing the national death toll to 14 for the year, according to state health officials. Pennsylvania reported its ninth death on November 23 — an unvaccinated resident of Centre County — and Wisconsin reported its third on November 24, an adult in Lafayette County, following two earlier deaths in the state of an infant and a child. New York and Virginia have also reported deaths, including a 7-month-old baby in New York and a child between ages 0 and 4 in Virginia.

The national tally of measles cases is approaching 6,000, the highest since 1991. Transmission is widespread across 47 states and jurisdictions, with 43 outbreaks this year accounting for 96 percent of cases. Four states have case counts above 500; Pennsylvania leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide.

Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in the air for up to two hours, and up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will become ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they have been vaccinated or previously infected. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible individuals is growing.

Last week, international health authorities formally declared that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning the virus is now endemic. To prevent measles from establishing a foothold, vaccination rates must be 95 percent or higher. According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states meet or exceed the 95 percent threshold, and even in those states, pockets of undervaccinated communities remain.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO amid scandal; new details emerge
body: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday after a weekend of intense pressure from Trump administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump, who personally called the board to vouch for him. The return came just days after Nvidia's chairman had effectively ruled out Huang's reinstatement, and despite an ongoing scandal involving alleged violations of the company's code of conduct, a U.S. export-control probe, and multiple legal challenges. Huang had been ousted after revelations of an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, which is under investigation for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's advanced GPUs into China in violation of U.S. rules designed to slow Beijing's development of frontier AI.

In his first all-hands address since returning, Huang admitted to breaking Nvidia's code of conduct but stressed that no one is exempt from it, adding that violations do not automatically lead to termination. According to Wired, he said, 'Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments still matter.' Ethics experts note such a stance risks eroding employee pride. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, said younger workers are especially sensitive to ethical lapses: 'They're really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.' Plass added that companies typically remove executives after investigations and launch 'hearts-and-minds' campaigns to rebuild trust, though that playbook is harder when the CEO is seen as irreplaceable, as Huang is at Nvidia.

The central unresolved question is what Nvidia knew about the alleged chip diversion to China, and whether Huang's relationship with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances. Export-control attorneys told TechCrunch that investigators would likely probe what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about end users, beyond formal compliance statements. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, and Singapore began its own probe in 2025. On Monday, the U.S. added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a restricted trade list, and last week issued new rules barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China. Nvidia said it will stop selling licensed chips to China, hire its first compliance officer, and create a new board committee focused on export controls.

Multiple U.S. authorities are pressing ahead. Attorney General Todd Blanche described Nvidia as 'a good corporate citizen' and said it is not a target, but declined to answer questions about the Megaspeed investigation, which the Justice Department said is ongoing. California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the SEC are reportedly investigating Nvidia's corporate disclosures. Three House committees will privately interview Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week; the Senate Banking Committee will hold a public hearing on December 3. Senator Elizabeth Warren said the company and the Trump administration still owe Congress answers about compliance and the White House's role in Huang's reinstatement.

Legal actions are mounting. A potential class-action lawsuit was filed shortly after the scandal broke, followed by a shareholder derivative suit against Nvidia's directors, alleging they ignored red flags about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence source. Three more suits were filed on November 18. Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld called Nvidia 'a detriment to U.S. global industrial might,' arguing it has put sophisticated technology in the hands of adversaries. He warned that directors who approved Huang's return face a 'historic level of individual liability,' even as investors in both the U.S. and Asia welcomed the reinstatement—with one Chinese state-affiliated outlet running the headline 'The king is back!'
